Q: f-string W3School Challenge A:

The original template of the challenge is:

# The price
price = 49

# Use if...else inside f-string 
# to insert 'cheap' if the price is less than 50
# and insert 'expensive' otherwise.
txt = "It is very "

# Keep this print statement as it is
print(txt)

The correct answer should be:

# The price
price = 49

# Use if...else inside f-string 
# to insert 'cheap' if the price is less than 50
# and insert 'expensive' otherwise.
txt = "It is very {'expensive' if price>50 else 'cheap'}"

# Keep this print statement as it is
print(txt)

And yet you have removed the word very from the template, which causes the output to become It is cheap.

On-line tutorial / challenge sites like this expect the exact output from your code. If there's a single character different from the expectation, they would just report as error, even though your code logic is sound.

Its also quite common, while debugging a program, to feel as though you've hit an unbreakable wall. People often end up blaming the system such as suspecting the compiler is broken, the operating system has bugs, or similar issues. More often than not, the bug lurks in some trivial detail we've overlooked.

Q: Clear Formatting for a Range, not the Selection A:

Clear formats without modifying the selection.

Since the ClearFormatting method only works with the Selection object, to clear the formatting of a range without losing the selection, it is necessary to use the Range object instead of the Selection object:

Depending on what you want to do:

Clean up manual font formatting and character styles and restore the base paragraph style (restoring the "Default Paragraph Font" character formatting):

Range.Font.Reset

equivalent to

Range.Style = wdStyleDefaultParagraphFont

This can be done on any range:

  • The word the cursor is on :
Selection.Font.Reset
  • Selected range:
Selection.Range.Font.Reset

NOTE: It has no effect if the range is empty (IP cursor).

  • First or only paragraph of the selection:
Selection.Paragraphs(1).Range.Font.Reset
  • For a selection of several paragraphs, you need to expand the range:
Set rng = Selection.Range
rng.Expand wdParagraph 'We expand the range without affecting the selection.
rng.Font.Reset
  • For the whole book, as Greedo wants :
ActiveDocument.Range.Font.Reset

Clear paragraph formatting and paragraph style, and apply the "Normal" paragraph style:

IMPORTANT: This does not affect the font format or the applied character style!

  • To the paragraphs of the selection:
Selection.Paragraphs.Style = “Normal”
  • To the paragraphs of the range:
Range.Paragraphs.Style = “Normal”
  • To the entire document:
ActiveDocument.Range.Paragraphs.Style = “Normal”

Clean up manual paragraph formatting:

Restores paragraph formatting to the paragraph style, but does not modify manual font formatting or applied character styles..

Selection.Paragraphs.Reset

Range.Paragraphs.Reset

ActiveDocument.Paragraphs.Reset

After studying the documentation and much trial and error, I have been able to compile some notes on the use of styles in Word, which I share below:

Using Word Styles with VBA

The basic concept to understand is that Word's style and formatting system relies on a series of superimposed layers, which modify one another as you move up the levels, as explained in this old Microsoft blog:

https://web.archive.org/web/20120119103920/http://blogs.office.com/b/microsoft-word/archive/2008/10/16/behind-the-curtain-styles-order-of-operations.aspx#fbid=KpHwtjbzM_7

The first layer of formatting, the most basic one, consists of the document's default configuration for font and paragraph formats.

In other words, every document has a DEFAULT CONFIGURATION for font and paragraph formats, which forms the basis of the document's formatting.

SETTING DEFAULT VALUES:

The default formatting configuration can be modified via the Word interface:

HOME Tab / Styles / Manage Styles / Set Defaults

This form allows you to set the default values for the document's font and paragraph formatting.

IMPORTANT:

-  This default configuration determines the "Normal" style, because this style is based on the document's default values.

-  Modifying the default configuration adjusts and modifies the "Normal" style.

-  However, the opposite does not occur: modifying the "Normal" style does not update or modify the default configuration, which can only be changed through the interface.

NOTE: That is to say, the document's default formatting values CANNOT be set via code!.

-  Therefore, the first step when creating a Document or Template should be to establish the default formatting values, as these values determine the formatting of the document's base style ("Normal" style).

OVERLAID LAYERS AND APPLICATION ORDER OF STYLE TYPES AND FORMATS:

Styles in Word are applied through layers that modify each other.

The logic of style superposition in Word works as follows:

-  Firstly, the default configuration of paragraph and font formats is applied.

-  Table style: within a table, table styles modify the document's default paragraph and character formats.

-  Paragraph style: sets formats that affect the entire paragraph.

-  Numbering style: determines the formatting of numbered lists, taking precedence over paragraph formatting.

-  Character style: only affects the font formatting of the range to which it is applied; however, for that range, the character formatting is superimposed and dominates over the paragraph's font formatting.

-  Manual paragraph and font formatting: these dominate over all others.

STYLES: ActiveDocument.Styles()

A collection of objects representing the built-in and user-defined styles in a document.

Style Types: Style.Type (Read-only)

ActiveDocument.Styles(stl).Type

Returns the style type (WdStyleType):

-  wdStyleTypeParagraph ("¶"): 1 Paragraph style. Controls alignment, line spacing, and fonts for the entire paragraph. The "Normal" style is a paragraph style.

-  wdStyleTypeCharacter ("a"): 2 Independent text character style. Applied only to a selection of text (such as bold or colour).

-  wdStyleTypeTable: 3 Table style. Defines borders, shading, and fonts for cells within a table.

-  wdStyleTypeList: 4 List style. Defines outline levels, bullets, and numbering.

-  wdStyleTypeLinked ("¶a"): 5 Linked styles. Can be applied as both characters and to entire paragraphs. For example, Heading styles.

NOTE on Linked Styles:

The linked style type (wdStyleTypeLinked) is the only one that does not appear in the Style.Type property, which in these styles is wdStyleTypeParagraph (paragraph style type).

To verify if a style is linked, you must check the property:

Selection.Style.Linked or Selection.Range.Style.Linked

(True/False/Not Available).

Disabling linked styles (wdStyleTypeLinked):

In the Word interface, there is an option called "Disable Linked Styles" so that linked styles (like headings) only function as PARAGRAPH styles, and not as character styles.This can also be done via code:

Application.RestrictLinkedStyles = False

PARAGRAPH STYLES (wdStyleTypeParagraph):

These affect the entire paragraph, from an entry point to the next "Enter" (paragraph end mark "¶").

They define the general structure of the entire paragraph (line spacing, alignment, size, font, etc.).

Applying a paragraph style:

To apply a paragraph style, it is not necessary to make a prior selection; the style can be applied directly to the paragraph or paragraphs of the Range object (including Selection.Range):

rng.Paragraphs.Style = paragraphStyle

Selection.Paragraphs.Style = paragraphStyle

Selection.Range.Paragraphs.Style = paragraphStyle

NOTE: The "Normal" style is a paragraph-type style.

Clearing manual paragraph formatting: (Paragraphs.Reset)

Removes manual paragraph formatting (formatting not applied by a style), but does not modify manual font formatting or character-type styles applied to paragraph ranges.

It can be applied to both Selection and Range:

Selection.Paragraphs.Reset

Selection.Paragraphs(p).ResetSet

Set rng = Selection.Range
rng.Paragraphs.Reset

CHARACTER STYLES (wdStyleTypeCharacter):

They act as a formatting "layer" that is applied only to individual letters or words or isolated ranges.

It overwrites specific font properties (colour, underline, bold, etc.) only in the range where it is applied.

Most common built-in (BuiltIn) Character Styles:

-  wdStyleEmphasis: Emphasis (Subtle italics).

-  wdStyleStrong:                     Strong (Pronounced bold).

-  wdStyleHyperlink: Hyperlink (Blue and underlined).

-  wdStyleFootnoteReference:  Footnote Ref. (Superscript for notes).

-  wdStylePageNumber:            Page Number (The formatting of the number in the footer).

Applying Character Styles:

rng.Style = "Character style"

Selection.Style = "Character style"

  • They only affect the selection or range.

  • When using Selection:

    - When a range is selected:

Selection.Style / Selection.Range.Style applies character formatting to the entire selected range

-  If NO range is selected (IP cursor):

Selection.Style:             Only affects the word where the cursor is placed!.

Selection.Range.Style:  Has no effect (null range).

Checking the Character Style applied to a range:

stl = .Range.CharacterStyle

IMPORTANT:

-  It is a read-only property.

-  It shows the character style (e.g., "Emphasis") associated with a range.

IMPORTANT: It does not exist for Selection, but only for its Range:

stl = Selection.Range.CharacterStyle

IMPORTANT: If the selected range has more than one character style, it returns Nothing!.

Clearing character style and manual font formatting:

Only affects the selection or range.

It is equivalent to applying the font of the underlying paragraph style ("Default Paragraph Font").

rng.Font.Reset

Selection.Font.Reset

Selection.Range.Font.Reset

rng.Style = wdStyleDefaultParagraphFont

Selection.Style = wdStyleDefaultParagraphFont

Selection.Range.Style = wdStyleDefaultParagraphFont

Q: Only final project in Project Group (bpg) runs correctly A:

Error 2 is "File Not Found". Now, it can be a bit misleading, as the file that it can't find isn't necessarily the .exe file, but could be a dependant .dll (or .bpl) file that is statically linked and that - with the PATH and current directory while running in IDE - doesn't allow Windows to find it, whereas when you run it manually outside the IDE your PATH and/or working (current) directory is different.

You can try setting the "Working Directory" to the same as the .EXE file in your projects' settings as this is most likely the working directory when you launch it manually, but it may be the IDE's working directory that is inherited by default in the application when you attempt to run it from within the IDE.

Q: how to run android on qemu A:

Do you have a specific need to run Android in QEMU and not use the emulator binary included with AOSP in prebuilts/android-emulator/linux-x86_64/emulator?

If so...

  • What command did you use to build AOSP?

  • What error did you encounter when running with QEMU?

  • What version of QEMU are you using?

  • What is your host Linux machine cat /etc/os-release?

Assuming on the other hand you actually just want to start the Android emulator for your build...

You don't need to run QEMU, there is a pre-built emulator binary (based on QEMU) include with AOSP already.

Did you read: https://source.android.com/docs/setup/create/avd ?

As explained there after building AOSP SDK you just need to run the following command:

$ emulator

If you run emulator --help there is a lot of helpful information.
